Working from the article directly. Here is the full analysis:

---

**Published online:**
September 3, 2026

**Geographic focus:**
United States

**Temporal focus:**
T1. Historical report [YES] — references trailing R-star data (Laubach-Williams model through Q2 2026) and the trajectory since Q1 2025
T2. Forward-looking reporting short-term risks (next few weeks/months) [YES] — ongoing bond selloff, yield pressure across the curve, Fed pause implications
T3. Forward-looking reporting long-term risks (next quarters/years) [YES] — structural shift in neutral rate, AI disinflationary flip, $40T debt trajectory, long-duration supply overhang

**Synopsis:**
The article argues that the current US Treasury selloff is being structurally amplified by a rising R-star (neutral/natural rate). The NY Fed's Laubach-Williams model pegs R-star at 1.65% as of Q2 2026, but market participants believe the true figure is materially higher due to two concurrent forces: (1) massive private capital demand from AI-driven hyperscaler bond issuance (Amazon, Microsoft, Google), and (2) heavy US government borrowing with national debt at $40 trillion. Together these are lifting real yields, compressing the Fed's ability to cut rates, and pushing term premiums higher — most acutely at the long end (30-year). A minority view holds that AI may eventually prove disinflationary, temporarily suppressing the neutral rate long-term, but analysts stress it is far too early to confirm a structural vs. cyclical shift.

---

**Q01. Is the content relevant to US economy, US yields, US interest rates and US market pricing?**
Relevance: YES — Directly addresses US Treasury yields across the curve (2Y, 5Y, 10Y, 30Y), Fed policy rate trajectory, term premium, and structural neutral rate dynamics.

**Q02. Is the content about increasing US interest rates?**
Relevance: 90 (strongly YES — the central thesis is that R-star is rising, pulling rates higher across the curve on a structural basis)
Increasing rates magnitude: No precise target rate given; R-star cited at 1.65% (Laubach-Williams Q2 2026, up from 1.36% in Q1 2025), with market consensus that the true level is higher still. No terminal rate figure explicitly stated.

**Q03. Is the content about holding stable US interest rates?**
Relevance: 40 — The article does reference a Fed on "extended pause" as a likely near-term scenario, but this is framed as a consequence of structural upward pressure, not a standalone stable-rates thesis.

**Q04. Is the content about decreasing US interest rates?**
Relevance: 15 — Cuts are discussed only as a constrained, distant possibility, contingent on AI proving disinflationary. The dominant message actively argues against near-term easing.
Decreasing rates magnitude: Not quantified; directionally dismissed as near-term unlikely.

**Q05. Focus on the very latest information: Is it striking a different sentiment/tone compared to previous discussions on US interest rates?**
Difference: +70 (Meaningfully more hawkish than before) — The article introduces a structural, supply-side driver for higher rates (AI capex + sovereign borrowing) that goes beyond the cyclical inflation narrative that dominated prior rate discussions. The framing of R-star as persistently elevated — not transiently elevated — is a hawkish escalation in tone.

**Q06. Focus on the very latest information: How does it compare to previous information on US interest rates?**
Difference: +65 (More hawkish than before) — Prior rate discourse centered on the Fed cutting as inflation normalized. This article shifts the conversation to a structurally higher neutral rate that limits how far the Fed can cut even in benign conditions, reinforcing a higher-for-longer regime with a new, forward-looking justification (AI investment cycle + fiscal dominance). This is a net hawkish delta relative to consensus that had been tilting toward eventual easing.
